title: UltraVoxelGS: 3D Ultrasound From Tracked Sweeps in Seconds
partialText:
Hong Kong Baptist University turns tracked 2D ultrasound frames into a 3D Gaussian scene in about 10 seconds, no per-scan fitting.

AI-assistance disclosure: I drafted this article with AI assistance, then edited it and fact-checked every number against the paper (arXiv:2611.11951).

Freehand 2D ultrasound is still how most abdominal, vascular and musculoskeletal scans get done, and the sonographer builds the 3D picture in their head. Nobody sees which part of the organ was never swept until the patient has left. A group at Hong Kong Baptist University wants to change that with a live 3D view that keeps up with the probe. Yue Wang, Haoxin Chen and Xiaoqing Guo built UltraVoxelGS, a network that turns a sequence of tracked 2D ultrasound frames into a renderable 3D Gaussian scene in about 10 seconds, with no per-scan training. The paper is arXiv:2611.11951 and is accepted at NeurIPS 2026.

UltraVoxelGS is feed-forward. Earlier neural ultrasound reconstructions such as UltraNeRF, ImplicitVol or Gaussian splatting fitted to one scan optimize a fresh model for every patient, which takes minutes. UltraVoxelGS predicts the whole scene in one pass of an already trained network.

What UltraVoxelGS does

The input is what a tracked ultrasound system already records: 2D B-mode frames, each with a probe pose from an optical tracker, an electromagnetic tracker or a robot arm. The output is a cloud of 3D Gaussians that you can slice at any probe position and angle, including ones the operator never held.

Feed-forward Gaussian methods from photography do not transfer, and the paper explains why. They assume many overlapping photos of the same surface that look alike from different angles. Two ultrasound frames share at most a line, and the same tissue looks different depending on where the sound comes from, because echoes are direction-dependent and the signal fades with depth. So UltraVoxelGS works in two steps.

First, it uses the poses to place every pixel of every frame in 3D and blends them into one fixed voxel grid (0.75 mm spacing in the paper). This is close to classic freehand compounding. Then a Transformer reads small 8 × 8 × 8 voxel patches and predicts Gaussians for them. It only predicts the thin slab of the grid around each frame, then averages Gaussians where slabs overlap. Because the network sees the grid and not the raw frames, the cost depends on the volume size rather than on the number of frames.

Each Gaussian stores a direction-dependent echo strength and an attenuation value. The renderer multiplies the echo by how much signal survives along the beam path, so a structure under a strong reflector can appear darker, as it does on a real scanner. Nobody labels attenuation. It is learned only by matching rendered frames to recorded ones.

The last piece is Render-time Appearance Adaptation. When you ask for a view, the method finds the recorded frame whose probe center is closest, briefly adjusts the appearance values (not the geometry) so the render matches that neighbour, renders, and throws the adjustment away. This step does most of the sharpening. Without it, the rendered slices look smoothed by the voxel grid.

What they found

The main real dataset is a public set of robot-held lumbar spine sweeps with probe tracking from 63 healthy volunteers, with over 3,000 frames per scan. The second is 100 simulated liver sweeps generated from abdominal CT volumes in 3D-IRCADb and CRLM-CT. The test is held-out frames: the method never sees them, and the render at that pose is compared with the recorded image.

Building the scene takes 10.04 seconds per spine case, against 10 minutes for per-scan Gaussian splatting (3DGS) and 15 to 18 minutes for UltraGauss and UltraNeRF. On the spine data UltraVoxelGS also renders the held-out frames best, with a PSNR of 24.29 dB against 22.55 dB for 3DGS. On the simulated liver it is ahead on PSNR and SSIM but not on LPIPS, where UltraNeRF scores better.

The same trained model handles about 300, 600 or 1,600 input frames without retraining, and peak memory stays under 4 GB. On the paired handheld sweeps from the same spine dataset, again without retraining, it stayed close to its robot-held score (23.96 against 24.29 dB). When the authors added large synthetic tracking errors (about 21 mm and 10 degrees RMS), quality dropped by about 1.4 dB, mostly because the wrong neighbour frame got picked for the appearance step. A streaming mode updates only the blocks touched by each new group of 10 frames and comes out almost identical to reconstructing the whole sweep at once.

Why a viewer or clinic team should care

If you build ultrasound software, coverage feedback is the obvious first use. The Gaussians only carry evidence where frames passed. In the failure-case figure, under very sparse coverage, ImplicitVol and UltraNeRF return dense but smeared or noisy texture, while UltraVoxelGS leaves the under-covered region visibly incomplete. For a coverage display, that is the behaviour you want, because the hole tells the operator where to go back.

Review after the exam is the next use. A 10-second reconstruction can run while the patient gets dressed, and the radiologist can then reslice the sweep along planes that were never acquired. The appendix contrasts this with commercial compounding, which averages every revisit into one isotropic voxel value and so favors slow, even sweeps. Keeping direction-dependent echoes means the operator can scan a spot from a second angle to see past a shadow, and the model keeps both views.

The output is an explicit set of Gaussians, which is easier to store and send than a neural field, though it needs a renderer that knows the attenuation model. Rendering one slice without the appearance step takes 3.6 ms. With the default 50 adaptation steps it is 623 ms, fine for review but not for a 30 fps live view.

What it does not tell you yet

It needs tracked frames. Without a tracker or a robot, you first need pose estimation from the images, and the paper does not test that.

Low resolution. Frames go in at 176 × 88 pixels, far below what a clinical display shows. The paper does not report results at native resolution.

Image quality, not diagnosis. Every number scores how well held-out frames are rendered, plus a SAM2-based liver segmentation check on the simulated data. Nothing measures whether a reader finds more or misses less.

Narrow anatomy. One real anatomy (lumbar spine in healthy volunteers) and one simulated organ. No patients with pathology, no cardiac motion, no breathing.

Hardware is unclear. The rendering timings were averaged across three V100 GPUs. The paper does not say what GPU produced the 10-second build, and training used one NVIDIA H20 for 300k iterations.

Simplified physics. The renderer models reflection and attenuation only. Speed-of-sound changes, refraction, speckle decorrelation and vendor post-processing are not modelled, as the authors state.

How to try it

Not yet. The repository YuebyYue/UltraVoxelGS-camera-ready currently holds a README that says “Code coming soon”, a citation, and no license file. Watch it if you want to test it on your own tracked sweeps. The spine dataset (Cavalcanti et al., Scientific Data 2025) is public under CC BY 4.0, so a team with a tracked probe can at least compare its own compounding against the figures in the paper.

For a related idea on the CT side, see our post on CTBakeGS (https://pycad.co/blog/ctbakegs-ct-volume-rendering-gaussian-splats/), which turns CT volumes into shareable Gaussian splat renderings. If your probe has no tracker, our post on estimating a six-DoF pose for untracked 2D ultrasound (https://pycad.co/blog/untracked-2d-ultrasound-six-dof-pose-on-3d-volume/) covers that missing step.

Source and license

Paper: Yue Wang, Haoxin Chen and Xiaoqing Guo, “UltraVoxelGS: Voxel-First Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for 3D Ultrasound Reconstruction”, Department of Computer Science, Hong Kong Baptist University, arXiv:2611.11951 (cs.CV, 9 November 2026), NeurIPS 2026. Code: github.com/YuebyYue/UltraVoxelGS-camera-ready, not yet released and with no license stated. Datasets: lumbar spine ultrasound from Cavalcanti et al. (CC BY 4.0); simulated liver sweeps built from 3D-IRCADb (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and CRLM-CT (CC BY 4.0) with the LOTUS simulator. Featured image: Fig. 5 of the paper, panels cropped and scaled.

Originally published on pycad.co, the canonical version: https://pycad.co/blog/ultravoxelgs-3d-ultrasound-tracked-sweeps-seconds/

title: A Dialog Can Close on Outside Click With No JavaScript. Most Developers Still Measure Clicks.
partialText:
Closing a modal when someone clicks outside it is usually a click handler that compares coordinates or checks `event.target`. The `closedby` attribute on `<dialog>` does it in the browser. It works in Chrome and Edge 134 and Firefox 141, and the compatibility data I read has no Safari entry. I tested the old handlers and the attribute side by side, and the old handlers failed in four ways I didn’t expect.

I want to describe a snippet I’d guess is in most codebases that have a modal.

You want the dialog to close when someone clicks the dark area behind it. A `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()` doesn’t do that by default, so you searched for it and pasted this:

dlg.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
 if (event.target === dlg) dlg.close();
});

The idea is that a click on the backdrop reports the dialog itself as its target, and a click on the content reports something inside it. It works when you click the backdrop. I made the test dialog look like a real one, with 40px of padding, and then did what real users do:

- I clicked in the padding. The dialog closed. The padding belongs to the dialog element, so the click’s target was the dialog, and the handler read it as an outside click.
- I selected text and let go outside. I pressed the mouse button on a paragraph inside the dialog, dragged out past the edge and released on the backdrop. The dialog closed, in the middle of selecting text.

The other popular version measures the click against the dialog’s box:

dlg.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
 const r = dlg.getBoundingClientRect();
 const inside =
 event.clientX >= r.left && event.clientX <= r.right &&
 event.clientY >= r.top && event.clientY <= r.bottom;
 if (!inside) dlg.close();
});

That one survived the padding. It failed the drag in the same way, and it failed a third test that I think is the nastier one. I focused a button inside the dialog and pressed Enter. The dialog closed. A click that comes from the keyboard has no pointer position, and the event I logged had `clientX` and `clientY` both at 0, so the check decided the click was in the corner of the page, outside the dialog. Every keyboard user who pressed Enter on a button in your modal closed it.

Here is the same behavior with no handler:

<dialog id="settings" closedby="any">
 <p>Settings go here.</p>
 <button commandfor="settings" command="close">Close</button>
</dialog>

I ran all four tests against that. Clicking the backdrop closed it. The padding click, the drag and the Enter key did not.

What `closedby` does

The attribute says which user actions can close the dialog. MDN describes three kinds: a light dismiss (clicking outside), a platform action such as Esc, and a mechanism you provide, such as a button. It takes three values:

- `any`: all three.
- `closerequest`: the platform action and your own mechanism, with no light dismiss.
- `none`: only your own mechanism.

If you leave it out, a dialog opened with `showModal()` behaves like `closerequest`, and any other dialog behaves like `none`. I checked the defaults in Chrome 153. A modal with no attribute closed on Esc and ignored a backdrop click. With `closedby=”none”`, Esc did nothing. The `closedBy` property on the element reflected the attribute, and setting it to `any` from script was enough to turn on the backdrop click.

One honest note first. For a plain “click outside to close” on a modal, `closedby=”any”` is the whole change. Everything below is what else the attribute lets you say.

Use case 1: close on outside click, correctly

That’s the `closedby=”any”` dialog from the opening, and the part worth repeating is what the browser doesn’t do. Pressing the mouse inside the dialog and releasing outside, which closed both old versions, left `closedby=”any”` open. So did the padding and the keyboard. The attribute isn’t smarter than your handler in a magical way. It just tracks where the press started and ended, which is the thing the handlers were approximating.

Use case 2: a dialog that can’t be dismissed by accident

<dialog id="confirm" closedby="none">
 <p>Delete this project? This can't be undone.</p>
 <button commandfor="confirm" command="close">Cancel</button>
 <button>Delete</button>
</dialog>

With `closedby=”none”`, pressing Esc left the dialog open, and so did a backdrop click. It closed only through the Cancel button. That’s right for a choice the user has to make. MDN’s advice applies: provide a closing control on every dialog, and especially on this one, because a person without a physical keyboard has no Esc.

Use case 3: a guard for unsaved changes

Light dismiss goes through the same `cancel` event as Esc, so a form with unsaved changes can stop it:

dlg.addEventListener("cancel", (event) => {
 if (isDirty) event.preventDefault();
});

I clicked the backdrop of a dialog with that listener, with `isDirty` true, five times in a row. Each click fired `cancel`, and the dialog stayed open all five times. With `isDirty` false, a click fired `cancel` and then `close`.

Esc behaved differently, and you should know it. With the same listener calling `preventDefault()`, I pressed Esc five times. The first two presses left the dialog open. The third one closed it, even though the handler had canceled that one too. I didn’t dig into why, but it means `cancel` is a way to ask for a pause, not a lock. If losing the data would hurt, save a draft as well.

Use case 4: a non-modal panel that dismisses itself

`closedby` isn’t only for modals. A dialog opened with `show()` stays non-modal, so the page behind it remains usable:

<dialog id="panel" closedby="any">
 <p>Filters</p>
</dialog>
panel.show();

With `closedby=”any”`, clicking elsewhere on the page closed the panel. So did Esc with focus inside it, and so did clicking another button on the page. With no attribute, none of those closed it, because a non-modal dialog defaults to `none`. With `closedby=”closerequest”`, only Esc closed it. That makes a non-modal dialog behave like an `auto` popover, with the extra things a dialog can do.

Use case 5: it works with no JavaScript at all

Combine it with the invoker commands from my previous article and the dialog needs no script to open or close:

<button commandfor="settings" command="show-modal">Settings</button>
<dialog id="settings" closedby="any">
 <p>Settings go here.</p>
 <button commandfor="settings" command="close">Close</button>
</dialog>

I opened it with the button and clicked the backdrop, and it closed with no script on the page. I repeated the test with JavaScript disabled, and the dialog still opened and still closed on a backdrop click.

Progressive enhancement

Not every browser has it, so a small fallback makes sense for the ones that don’t:

if (!("closedBy" in HTMLDialogElement.prototype)) {
 let pressedOutside = false;
const isOutside = (event) => {
 const dialog = event.target;
 if (!(dialog instanceof HTMLDialogElement)) return false;
 if (dialog.getAttribute("closedby") !== "any") return false;
 const r = dialog.getBoundingClientRect();
 return (
 event.clientX < r.left || event.clientX > r.right ||
 event.clientY < r.top || event.clientY > r.bottom
 );
 };
document.addEventListener("pointerdown", (event) => {
 pressedOutside = isOutside(event);
 });
document.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
 if (pressedOutside && isOutside(event)) event.target.close();
 pressedOutside = false;
 });
}

It remembers where the press started, and it only acts on clicks whose target is the dialog itself, which rules out the keyboard click that broke the second old version. It handles only `any`, and only for the backdrop click.

I couldn’t run a browser without `closedBy`. To test the logic, I forced the check to true and read a `data-closedby` attribute instead, so Chrome’s own light dismiss wouldn’t interfere. In that setup the backdrop click closed the dialog, and the padding click, the drag and the Enter key did not. That tests the fallback’s logic, not Safari.

Browser support: the honest picture

The `web-features` data, version 3.44.0, lists `closedby` as supported from Chrome and Edge 134 and Firefox 141, on desktop and Android. It has no Safari entry, and the feature isn’t marked Baseline. I read that data and MDN’s page, and I didn’t test Firefox or Safari myself.

That’s the main caveat. Anyone on Safari gets no light dismiss from the attribute, so for a feature the dialog needs, keep a fallback or accept that Safari users close it with the button. The spec link in the data points to the HTML Standard.

I ran every example in Chrome 153. I’d planned to test an older version as well, and the older build was no longer available in my environment, so this round is a single Chrome version.

Gotchas worth knowing before you ship

The default for a modal is `closerequest`. Without the attribute, Esc closes a modal and a backdrop click doesn’t. If you want a click outside to work, you have to say `any`.

The padding counts as inside. A click in the dialog’s own padding didn’t close it. If you want a click on that area to count as outside, the attribute won’t do it.

Light dismiss fires `cancel`. That’s what makes the unsaved-changes guard in use case 3 work. It also means a shared `cancel` listener runs for backdrop clicks, not only for Esc.

Esc can’t be blocked forever. In my test the third press closed the dialog even with `preventDefault()` on every `cancel` event. A backdrop click was stopped every time, five out of five.

`none` needs a way out. A dialog the user can’t close with Esc or a click needs a visible button, and it still needs to work for someone without a keyboard.

On a non-modal dialog, other clicks close it. With `any`, clicking another button on the page closed the panel. That’s the point of the feature, but it surprised me the first time.

It isn’t in Safari’s data yet. The fallback above covers the backdrop click, and nothing else about the attribute.

How to think about this right now

For a modal that should close on an outside click, use `closedby=”any”`, and keep the fallback behind the feature check until your support matrix lets you delete it.

For a choice the user must make, use `closedby=”none”` and give the dialog a clear button. For a form with unsaved changes, add the `cancel` guard, and save a draft too.

If your handler works and nobody has complained, leave it. The next time someone reports that Enter closed the dialog, or that selecting text did, that’s the moment to switch.

A modal was always a place where the browser knew what the click was doing. It can decide whether the click counted.

This is part of my series on practical web development in 2026. Next: the CSS custom highlight API, and highlighting search matches without wrapping text in `<mark>`.
